chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter XXI
paragraphs: The wind had died down and black clouds, blending with the gun smoke, hung low over the battlefield on the horizon. It was getting dark, and the glow of two fires became more visible. The cannon fire was fading, but the crackle of muskets behind them and to the right was growing louder and closer. As soon as Tushin and his guns, constantly swerving around or encountering wounded men, made it out of firing range and down into the hollow, he was met by several staff officers, including the staff officer and Zherkov, who had been sent to Tushin's battery twice but had never actually reached it. Talking over each other, they all issued orders about what to do next, scolding and blaming him. Tushin gave no orders and rode silently behind on his artillery horse, afraid to speak because he felt ready to cry at every word without knowing why. Although the orders were to leave the wounded behind, many of them dragged themselves after the troops and begged for rides on the gun carriages. The lively infantry officer who had rushed out of Tushin's hut just before the battle was now lying on 'Matvyevna's' carriage with a bullet in his stomach. At the foot of the hill, a pale hussar cadet, holding one hand with the other, came up to Tushin and asked for a seat.
"Captain, please! I've hurt my arm," he said timidly. "Please... I can't walk. Please!"
It was clear that this cadet had already asked for a ride several times and been refused. He spoke in a hesitant, pitiful voice.
"Please, give me a seat!"
"Give him a seat," said Tushin. "Lay a cloak down for him to sit on, lad," he told his favorite soldier. "And where is the wounded officer?"
"He's been put down. He died," someone answered.
"Help him up. Sit down, friend, sit down! Spread out the cloak, Antonov."

The cadet was Rostov. He was supporting one hand with the other, his face was pale and his jaw trembled with feverish shivering. They placed him on 'Matvyevna,' the gun from which the dead officer had been removed. The cloak they spread under him was wet with blood that stained his pants and arm.
"What's the matter, are you wounded, son?" said Tushin, approaching the gun where Rostov sat.
"No, it's a sprain."
"Then what's this blood on the gun carriage?" asked Tushin.
"It was the officer, sir, who stained it," answered the artilleryman, wiping the blood away with his sleeve, as if apologizing for the state of his gun.

They could barely get the guns up the hill with the infantry's help, and when they reached the village of Gruntersdorf, they stopped. It had grown so dark that you couldn't tell uniforms apart from ten paces away, and the firing had begun to die down. Suddenly, close by on the right, shouting and shooting broke out again. Flashes of gunfire gleamed in the darkness. This was the last French attack, and it was met by soldiers who had taken shelter in the village houses. They all rushed out of the village again, but Tushin's guns couldn't move, and the artillerymen, Tushin, and the cadet exchanged silent glances as they waited for their fate. The firing died down and soldiers came streaming out of a side street, talking excitedly.
"You okay, Petrov?" asked one.
"We really let them have it! They won't try again now," said another.
"You couldn't see a thing. They were shooting at their own men! Total darkness, brother! Got anything to drink?"
The French had been driven back for the last time. And once again, in the total darkness, Tushin's guns moved forward, surrounded by the humming infantry like a frame around a picture.

In the darkness, it felt as though a gloomy, invisible river was flowing in one direction, humming with whispers and talk and the sound of hooves and wheels. Above the general rumble, the groans and voices of the wounded could be heard more clearly than anything else in the darkness of the night. Their groans seemed to merge with the darkness itself. After a while, the moving mass grew agitated. Someone rode past on a white horse with his staff and said something as he passed. "What did he say? Where are we going now? Are we stopping? Did he thank us?" came eager questions from all sides. The whole mass began pressing closer together, and word spread that they had been ordered to halt—evidently those in front had stopped. Everyone stayed where they were in the middle of the muddy road.

Fires were lit and the conversations grew louder. Captain Tushin, after giving orders to his company, sent a soldier to find a field hospital or a doctor for the cadet, and sat down by a bonfire the soldiers had built on the road. Rostov also dragged himself to the fire. From the pain, cold, and dampness, feverish shivers shook his whole body. Drowsiness was overpowering him, but he stayed awake because of the agonizing pain in his arm, for which he could find no comfortable position. He kept closing his eyes and then looking at the fire again, which seemed blindingly red, and at the small, round-shouldered figure of Tushin sitting cross-legged like a Turk beside him. Tushin's large, kind, intelligent eyes were fixed on Rostov with sympathy and compassion. Rostov could see that Tushin wanted with his whole heart to help but couldn't.

From all sides came the footsteps and voices of infantry walking, driving past, and settling in all around. The sounds of voices, tramping feet, horses' hooves in the mud, and crackling fires near and far merged into one trembling rumble.

It was no longer a dark, unseen river flowing through the gloom, but a dark sea gradually settling after a storm. Rostov looked and listened listlessly to what was happening around him. An infantryman came to the fire, squatted down, held his hands to the flames, and turned away.
"You don't mind, sir?" he asked Tushin. "I've lost my company, sir. I don't know where... what rotten luck!"

Along with the soldier, an infantry officer with a bandaged cheek came up to the fire and asked Tushin to move the guns slightly to let a wagon through. After he left, two soldiers rushed up to the campfire, fighting desperately over a boot they had both grabbed.
"You found it? Yeah right! Real clever!" one of them shouted hoarsely.
Then a thin, pale soldier with a bloody bandage around his neck came up and angrily asked the artillerymen for water.
"Do I have to die like a dog?" he said.
Tushin told them to give the man some water. Then a cheerful soldier ran up, asking for a bit of fire for the infantry.
"A nice little torch for the infantry! Good luck, fellow countrymen. Thanks for the fire—we'll pay it back with interest," he said, carrying a glowing stick off into the darkness.
Next came four soldiers carrying something heavy on a cloak, and they passed by the fire. One of them stumbled.
"Who the hell put those logs on the road?" he snarled.
"He's dead—why carry him?" said another.
"Shut up!"
And they disappeared into the darkness with their burden.
"Still hurting?" Tushin asked Rostov in a whisper.
"Yes."
"Sir, the general wants you. He's in the hut over there," said a gunner, coming up to Tushin.
"Coming, friend."
Tushin got up, buttoned his greatcoat, straightened it, and walked away from the fire.

Not far from the artillery campfire, in a hut that had been prepared for him, Prince Bagration sat at dinner, talking with several commanding officers who had gathered at his quarters. The little old man with half-closed eyes was there, greedily gnawing a mutton bone. The general who had served blamelessly for twenty-two years was there too, flushed from a glass of vodka and dinner. So was the staff officer with the signet ring, and Zherkov, glancing uneasily at everyone, and Prince Andrew, pale, with tight lips and feverishly bright eyes.

In a corner of the hut stood a captured French standard, and the accountant with the innocent face was fingering its fabric, shaking his head in confusion—perhaps because the banner genuinely interested him, or perhaps because it was hard for him, hungry as he was, to watch a dinner where there was no place for him. In the next hut was a French colonel who had been captured by their dragoons. Officers were crowding in to look at him. Prince Bagration was thanking the individual commanders and asking about the details of the battle and their losses. The general whose regiment had been inspected at Braunau was telling the prince that as soon as the fighting began, he had pulled back from the woods, gathered the men who were cutting timber, let the French pass, and then made a bayonet charge with two battalions that broke up the French troops.

"When I saw, your excellency, that their first battalion was falling apart, I stopped on the road and thought: 'I'll let them come closer and then hit them with the full firepower of the battalion'—and that's exactly what I did."

The general had wanted so badly to do this and was so sorry he hadn't managed to that he had come to believe it had actually happened. Perhaps it really had? Who could sort out what did or didn't happen in all that chaos?

"By the way, your excellency, I should mention," he continued, remembering Dolokhov's conversation with Kutuzov and his last encounter with the soldier, "that Private Dolokhov, who was demoted to the ranks, captured a French officer right in front of me and showed exceptional courage."

"I saw the Pavlograd hussars attack there, your excellency," Zherkov chimed in, looking around nervously. He hadn't actually seen the hussars all day but had heard about them from an infantry officer. "They broke through two enemy formations, your excellency."

Several people smiled at Zherkov's words, expecting one of his usual jokes, but when they realized what he said reflected well on their forces and the day's work, they put on serious expressions—even though many of them knew it was a complete fabrication. Prince Bagration turned to the old colonel:

"Gentlemen, I thank you all. Every branch has performed heroically—infantry, cavalry, and artillery. But how were two guns left behind in the center?" he asked, looking around for someone. (Prince Bagration didn't ask about the guns on the left flank; he already knew they had all been abandoned at the very start of the battle.) "I believe I sent you?" he added, turning to the staff officer on duty.
"One was damaged," the staff officer answered, "and the other I can't explain. I was there the whole time, giving orders, and had only just left... It's true it was intense there," he added modestly.
Someone mentioned that Captain Tushin was camped nearby and had already been sent for.
"Oh, but you were there?" said Prince Bagration, turning to Prince Andrew.
"Of course—we just barely missed each other," said the staff officer with a smile to Bolkonsky.
"I didn't have the pleasure of seeing you," said Prince Andrew, coldly and sharply.

Everyone fell silent. Tushin appeared in the doorway and made his way timidly past the generals in the crowded hut, embarrassed as he always was around his superiors. He didn't notice the standard's staff and tripped over it. Several people laughed.
"How was it that a gun was abandoned?" asked Bagration, frowning—not so much at the captain as at those who were laughing, especially Zherkov, who laughed loudest.

Only now, faced with the stern authorities, did the full horror of his guilt and the disgrace of having lost two guns while still being alive hit Tushin. He had been so caught up in the action that he hadn't thought about it until this moment. The officers' laughter confused him even more. He stood before Bagration with his lower jaw trembling, barely able to stammer: "I don't know... your excellency... I had no men... your excellency."
"You could have taken some from the covering troops."

Tushin didn't say that there had been no covering troops, even though that was completely true. He was afraid of getting another officer in trouble and silently fixed his eyes on Bagration, like a schoolboy who has made a mistake staring at the examiner.

The silence lasted for some time. Prince Bagration, apparently not wanting to be harsh, couldn't find anything to say. The others didn't dare to step in. Prince Andrew looked at Tushin from under his brows, his fingers twitching nervously.

"Your excellency!" Prince Andrew broke the silence with his sharp voice. "You sent me to Captain Tushin's battery. I went there and found two-thirds of the men and horses killed or wounded, two guns destroyed, and no support whatsoever."
Prince Bagration and Tushin both stared intently at Bolkonsky, who spoke with barely controlled emotion.

"And, if your excellency will allow me to say so," he continued, "we owe today's success mainly to the action of that battery and the heroic endurance of Captain Tushin and his men." Without waiting for a reply, Prince Andrew stood up and left the table.

Prince Bagration looked at Tushin. He was clearly reluctant to distrust Bolkonsky's passionate opinion, yet not quite able to fully accept it either. He nodded and told Tushin he could go. Prince Andrew walked out with him.
"Thank you—you saved me, my friend!" said Tushin.
Prince Andrew glanced at him but said nothing and walked away. He felt sad and depressed. It was all so strange, so unlike what he had hoped for.

"Who are they? Why are they here? What do they want? And when will all this end?" thought Rostov, watching the shifting shadows before him. The pain in his arm grew worse and worse. Unstoppable drowsiness overcame him. Red rings danced before his eyes, and the impression of those voices and faces and a feeling of loneliness merged with the physical pain. It was they, these soldiers—wounded and unwounded—who were crushing, pressing down, and twisting the muscles and burning the flesh of his sprained arm and shoulder. To escape them, he closed his eyes.

For a moment he dozed off, but in that brief interval countless things appeared to him in a dream: his mother and her large white hand, Sonya's thin little shoulders, Natasha's eyes and laughter, Denisov with his voice and mustache, and Telyanin and that whole affair with Telyanin and Bogdanich. That affair was the same thing as this soldier with the harsh voice, and it was that affair and this soldier that kept agonizingly, relentlessly pulling and pressing his arm, always dragging it in one direction. He tried to get away from them, but they wouldn't let his shoulder move even a hair's breadth. It wouldn't hurt—it would be fine—if only they would stop pulling it, but he couldn't get rid of them.

He opened his eyes and looked up. The black canopy of night hung less than a yard above the glow of the coals. Flakes of falling snow drifted through the light. Tushin hadn't come back, the doctor hadn't come. He was alone now, except for a soldier sitting naked on the other side of the fire, warming his thin yellow body.
"Nobody wants me!" thought Rostov. "There is no one to help me or feel sorry for me. Yet I was once at home, strong, happy, and loved." He sighed and, as he did, groaned involuntarily.
"Hey, something hurting you?" asked the soldier, shaking out his shirt over the fire. Without waiting for an answer, he grunted and added: "What a lot of men got mangled today—terrible!"

Rostov wasn't listening. He watched the snowflakes fluttering above the fire and remembered a Russian winter at his warm, bright home, his fluffy fur coat, his sleigh gliding quickly along, his healthy body, and all the love and care of his family. "Why did I come here?" he wondered.
The next day the French did not attack again, and the remnants of Bagration's force rejoined Kutuzov's army.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter I
paragraphs: Prince Vasili was not a man who carefully planned things out. Even less did he deliberately scheme to hurt anyone for his own benefit. He was simply a man of the world who had learned how to get ahead, and getting ahead had become second nature to him. Plans and strategies that he never quite acknowledged to himself, but that made up the entire interest of his life, were constantly forming in his mind, sparked by the people and situations he encountered. He didn't have just one or two such plans going at once, but dozens—some barely taking shape, some nearing completion, and some already falling apart. He never said to himself, for instance, 'This man has influence, so I need to win his trust and use him to get a special appointment.' Nor did he think, 'Pierre is rich, so I should get him to marry my daughter and lend me forty thousand rubles.' But whenever he met someone powerful, his instincts immediately told him that person could be useful, and without any forethought, Prince Vasili would seize the first opportunity to gain his confidence, flatter him, become close to him, and eventually make his request.

He had Pierre right there in Moscow, so he arranged an appointment for him as Gentleman of the Bedchamber—which at the time carried the status of Councilor of State—and insisted the young man come with him to Petersburg and stay at his house. With what looked like absent-mindedness, yet with unwavering confidence that he was doing the right thing, Prince Vasili did everything to get Pierre to marry his daughter. If he had actually planned it all out, he couldn't have been so natural or shown such relaxed familiarity with people both above and below him in social standing. Something always drew him toward those richer and more powerful than himself, and he had a rare talent for choosing exactly the right moment to use people.

Pierre, who had unexpectedly become Count Bezukhov and a rich man, felt so overwhelmed after his recent loneliness and freedom that he could only be by himself in bed. He had to sign papers, visit government offices whose purpose he didn't understand, consult his head steward, inspect his estate near Moscow, and receive a stream of people who had previously ignored his existence but would now have been offended if he hadn't seen them. All of these people—businessmen, relatives, acquaintances—treated the young heir with the greatest friendliness and flattery. They were all obviously convinced of Pierre's fine qualities. He kept hearing things like: 'With your remarkable kindness,' or 'With your excellent heart,' 'You are such an honorable man, Count,' or 'If only he were as clever as you.' He began to genuinely believe in his own exceptional kindness and extraordinary intelligence, especially since, deep down, he had always felt he really was kind and intelligent. Even people who had been unfriendly before now became warm and affectionate. The stern eldest princess, with her long waist and doll-like plastered-down hair, had come to Pierre's room after the funeral. With lowered eyes and frequent blushes, she told him she was sorry about their past disagreements and now felt she had no right to ask anything—only permission, after the blow she had suffered, to stay a few more weeks in the house she loved so much and where she had sacrificed so much. She couldn't hold back her tears. Moved by this transformation in the stiff princess, Pierre took her hand and begged her forgiveness, without knowing what for. From that day on, the eldest princess completely changed toward Pierre and even began knitting him a striped scarf.
"Do this for me, my dear—after all, she had to put up with a great deal from the deceased," said Prince Vasili, handing Pierre a document to sign for the princess's benefit.

Prince Vasili had decided it was necessary to throw this bone—a thirty-thousand-ruble payment—to the poor princess, so it wouldn't occur to her to talk about his role in the affair of the inlaid portfolio. Pierre signed the document, and after that the princess became even kinder. The younger sisters also grew affectionate toward him, especially the youngest, the pretty one with the mole, who often made him feel flustered with her smiles and her own blushing whenever they met.

It seemed so natural to Pierre that everyone liked him, and it would have seemed so strange if anyone hadn't, that he couldn't help believing in the sincerity of those around him. Besides, he was always busy and felt in a constant state of mild, cheerful excitement. He felt like the center of some important movement—that people were always expecting something of him, that if he didn't deliver he would disappoint many people, but if he just did this and that, everything would be fine. And so he did what was asked of him, but that happy outcome always remained somewhere in the future.

More than anyone, Prince Vasili took charge of Pierre's affairs and of Pierre himself during those early days. From the death of Count Bezukhov, he never let go of the young man. He had the manner of someone burdened with business, weary and suffering, who nevertheless wouldn't abandon this helpless youth—after all, the son of his old friend and the owner of such enormous wealth—to the whims of fate and the schemes of villains. During his few days in Moscow after Count Bezukhov's death, he would summon Pierre or visit him, telling him what needed to be done in a tired, confident tone, as if adding each time: 'You know I'm overwhelmed with work and it's purely out of kindness that I bother with you, and you know perfectly well that what I'm proposing is the only sensible option.'

"Well, my dear fellow, tomorrow we're off at last," said Prince Vasili one day, closing his eyes and touching Pierre's elbow, speaking as if they had agreed on this long ago and it couldn't be changed. "We leave tomorrow and I'm giving you a place in my carriage. I'm very glad. All our important business here is settled, and I should have left ages ago. Here's something I received from the chancellor. I asked him on your behalf, and you've been accepted into the diplomatic corps and made a Gentleman of the Bedchamber. A diplomatic career now lies open before you."

Despite the weary confidence with which these words were delivered, Pierre, who had been thinking about his future for a long time, wanted to say something. But Prince Vasili cut him off in that special deep, cooing tone he used in extreme cases when special persuasion was needed—a tone that made interruption impossible.

"But my dear, I did this for my own sake, to satisfy my conscience, and there's nothing to thank me for. No one has ever complained about being loved too much. Besides, you're free—you could drop the whole thing tomorrow. But you'll see everything for yourself when you get to Petersburg. It's time you got away from these terrible memories." Prince Vasili sighed. "Yes, yes, my boy. And my valet can ride in your carriage. Oh, I nearly forgot," he added. "You know, my dear, your father and I had some financial matters between us, so I've collected what was due from the Ryazan estate and I'll keep it. You won't be needing it. We'll sort out the accounts later."
By 'what was due from the Ryazan estate,' Prince Vasili meant several thousand rubles in rent payments from Pierre's peasants, which the prince had pocketed for himself.

In Petersburg, as in Moscow, Pierre found the same atmosphere of warmth and friendliness. He couldn't refuse the position—or rather the rank, since he did nothing—that Prince Vasili had arranged for him. Social obligations, invitations, and engagements were so numerous that here, even more than in Moscow, he felt a sense of bewilderment, bustle, and constant expectation of something good that was always just ahead but never quite arrived.

Many of his former bachelor friends were no longer in Petersburg. The Guards had gone to the front. Dolokhov had been demoted to the ranks. Anatole was somewhere in the provinces with the army. Prince Andrew was abroad. So Pierre had no chance to spend his evenings the way he used to, or to have intimate, heart-to-heart conversations with an older friend he respected. His entire time was consumed by dinners and balls, mostly spent at Prince Vasili's house in the company of the stout princess, his wife, and their beautiful daughter Hélène.
Like everyone else, Anna Pavlovna Scherer showed Pierre the change in attitude that society had adopted toward him.

Before, in Anna Pavlovna's presence, Pierre had always felt that everything he said was out of place, tactless, and awkward—that remarks which seemed clever in his head sounded stupid the moment he spoke them, while Hippolyte's dumbest comments somehow came out witty and clever. Now everything Pierre said was charming. Even if Anna Pavlovna didn't say so directly, he could tell she wanted to and only held back out of respect for his modesty.
In the early winter of 1805-06, Pierre received one of Anna Pavlovna's usual pink invitations, with a note added: 'You will find the beautiful Hélène here, whom it is always a delight to see.'

When he read that line, Pierre felt for the first time that some connection that others could see had formed between him and Hélène. The thought both alarmed him—as if some obligation were being placed on him that he couldn't fulfill—and pleased him as an intriguing possibility.

Anna Pavlovna's party was like the previous one, except this time the novelty she offered her guests was not Mortemart but a diplomat fresh from Berlin, bringing the latest details about Emperor Alexander's visit to Potsdam and how the two great friends had pledged an unbreakable alliance to uphold justice against the enemy of mankind. Anna Pavlovna greeted Pierre with a touch of sadness, clearly referring to the young man's recent loss of his father (everyone felt obligated to remind Pierre how devastated he must be by the death of a father he had barely known), and her sadness matched the grand melancholy she displayed when mentioning Her Most August Majesty the Empress. Pierre felt flattered. Anna Pavlovna arranged the groups in her drawing room with her usual skill. The larger group, which included Prince Vasili and the generals, had the diplomat's attention. Another group gathered around the tea table. Pierre wanted to join the first, but Anna Pavlovna—in the excited state of a battlefield commander with a thousand brilliant ideas and not enough time to execute them all—spotted Pierre, touched his sleeve with her finger, and said:

"Wait, I have something in mind for you this evening." She glanced at Hélène and smiled. "My dear Hélène, be kind to my poor aunt who adores you. Go keep her company for ten minutes. And so it won't be too boring, here is the dear count, who I'm sure won't refuse to go with you."
The beauty went to the aunt, but Anna Pavlovna held Pierre back, looking as if she had some final essential instructions.

"Isn't she magnificent?" she said to Pierre, pointing to the stately beauty gliding away. "And such poise! For such a young woman, such perfect manners! It comes from the heart. The man who wins her will be lucky indeed. With her, even the most ordinary man would have a brilliant position in society. Don't you agree? I just wanted to hear your opinion." And Anna Pavlovna let Pierre go.
Pierre sincerely agreed about Hélène's perfect manners. Whenever he thought of Hélène, it was only of her beauty and her remarkable ability to appear silently dignified in any social setting.

The old aunt received the two young people in her corner but seemed more interested in hiding her adoration for Hélène and showing her fear of Anna Pavlovna. She looked at her niece as if asking what to do with these visitors. As she left them, Anna Pavlovna touched Pierre's sleeve again: "I hope you won't say it's boring at my house again." She glanced at Hélène.

Hélène smiled with a look that said she couldn't imagine anyone seeing her without being enchanted. The aunt coughed, swallowed, and told Hélène in French how pleased she was to see her, then turned to Pierre with the same greeting and the same look. In the middle of a halting, dull conversation, Hélène turned to Pierre with the beautiful, radiant smile she gave everyone. Pierre was so used to that smile, and it meant so little to him, that he paid no attention. The aunt was talking about a collection of snuffboxes that had belonged to Pierre's father, Count Bezukhov, and showed them her own. Princess Hélène asked to see the portrait of the aunt's husband on the lid.
"That's probably by Vinesse," said Pierre, naming a famous miniaturist, and he leaned over the table to take the snuffbox while trying to hear the conversation at the other table.

He half stood up, meaning to walk around, but the aunt handed him the snuffbox across Hélène's back. Hélène leaned forward to make room and looked back with a smile. She was wearing, as always at evening parties, a dress cut very low at the front and back, in the fashion of the time. Her bust, which had always seemed like marble to Pierre, was so close that his nearsighted eyes couldn't help noticing the living warmth of her neck and shoulders, so near his lips that he would only have had to bend his head slightly to touch them. He felt the warmth of her body, smelled her perfume, and heard the creaking of her corset as she moved. He no longer saw her marble beauty as a complete whole unified with her dress—instead, he saw all the charm of her body barely concealed by her clothing. And once he had seen this, he couldn't unsee it, just as you can't restore an illusion you've seen through.

"So you've never noticed before how beautiful I am?" Hélène seemed to say. "You hadn't realized I'm a woman? Yes, I am a woman who could belong to anyone—to you too," said her glance. And at that moment Pierre felt that Hélène not only could but must be his wife, and that it couldn't be any other way.

He knew this as surely as if he had been standing at the altar with her. How and when it would happen he didn't know; he didn't even know if it would be a good thing (he even felt, for some reason he couldn't explain, that it would be a bad thing), but he knew it would happen.

Pierre dropped his eyes, then raised them again, trying to see her once more as a distant beauty far removed from him—the way he had seen her every day until then. But he could no longer do it. He couldn't, just as a man who has mistaken a tuft of steppe grass for a tree through the mist can never see it as a tree again once he recognizes what it is. She was terribly close. She already had power over him. Between them there was no barrier except the barrier of his own will.
"Well, I'll leave you in your little corner," came Anna Pavlovna's voice. "I can see you're doing just fine there."
And Pierre, anxiously trying to remember if he'd done anything wrong, looked around with a blush. It seemed to him that everyone knew what had happened to him, just as he knew it himself.
A little later, when he joined the larger group, Anna Pavlovna said to him: "I hear you're renovating your Petersburg house?"
This was true. The architect had told him it was necessary, and Pierre, without knowing why, was having his enormous Petersburg mansion redone.

"That's a good thing, but don't move out of Prince Vasili's. It's good to have a friend like the prince," she said, smiling at Prince Vasili. "I know a thing or two about that, don't I? And you're still so young. You need advice. Don't be angry with me for exercising an old woman's privilege."

She paused, as women always do after mentioning their age. "If you marry, that will be a different matter," she continued, her glance linking them both. Pierre didn't look at Hélène and she didn't look at him. But she was just as terrifyingly close. He mumbled something and blushed.

When he got home, he couldn't sleep for a long time, thinking about what had happened. What had happened? Nothing. He had simply realized that the woman he had known since childhood—about whom he would say casually when her beauty was mentioned, 'Yes, she's good-looking'—he had realized that this woman could be his.

"But she's stupid. I've said so myself," he thought. "There's something wrong, something ugly, about the feeling she stirs in me. I've been told that her brother Anatole was in love with her and she with him, that there was a real scandal, and that's why he was sent away. Hippolyte is her brother... Prince Vasili is her father... This is wrong..." he reflected. But even as he thought this—and the thought was still incomplete—he caught himself smiling and realized a completely different train of thought had taken over. While thinking about her flaws, he was simultaneously dreaming about how she would be his wife, how she would love him and become entirely different, and how everything he had thought and heard about her might be false. And once again he saw her, not as Prince Vasili's daughter, but her whole body only veiled by its gray dress. "But no! Why didn't this occur to me before?" And again he told himself it was impossible, that there would be something unnatural, something dishonorable about this marriage. He remembered her past words and looks and the words and looks of those who had seen them together. He recalled Anna Pavlovna's comments about his house, remembered a thousand similar hints from Prince Vasili and others, and was seized with terror that he had somehow already bound himself to do something clearly wrong that he ought not to do. But even as he was convincing himself of this, in another part of his mind her image rose in all its feminine beauty.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter II
paragraphs: In November 1805, Prince Vasili had to make an inspection tour of four different provinces. He had arranged this for himself so he could visit his neglected estates at the same time, pick up his son Anatole from his regiment, and take him to visit old Prince Bolkonsky to arrange a match with the rich old man's daughter. But before leaving home for these new tasks, Prince Vasili had to settle things with Pierre, who had lately been spending whole days at home—that is, at Prince Vasili's house where he was staying—and had been absurd, excited, and foolish in Hélène's presence (as a man in love should be), but had not yet proposed.

"This is all very well, but it needs to be settled," Prince Vasili said to himself with a sorrowful sigh one morning, feeling that Pierre—who was so deeply indebted to him (but never mind that)—was not handling this situation properly. "Youth, foolishness... well, God be with him," he thought, savoring his own generosity, "but it has to come to a head. The day after tomorrow is Lelya's name day. I'll invite two or three people, and if he still doesn't understand what he's supposed to do, then it becomes my responsibility—yes, my responsibility. I am her father."

Six weeks after Anna Pavlovna's party, and after the sleepless night when Pierre had decided that marrying Hélène would be a disaster and he should avoid her and leave, Pierre—despite that decision—had not left Prince Vasili's house. He felt with horror that in everyone's eyes he was being drawn closer to her every day, that he could no longer see her the way he used to, that he couldn't break away from her, and that although it would be terrible, he would have to tie his fate to hers. He might have been able to free himself, but Prince Vasili—who had rarely hosted gatherings before—now threw a party almost every evening at which Pierre had to be present unless he wanted to spoil everyone's enjoyment and disappoint their expectations. In the rare moments when he was home, Prince Vasili would take Pierre's hand in passing and draw it downward, or absent-mindedly offer his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek for Pierre to kiss, saying: 'See you tomorrow,' or 'Come to dinner or I won't see you,' or 'I'm staying in just for your sake.' And although Prince Vasili, when he stayed in 'for Pierre's sake,' barely exchanged two words with him, Pierre felt he couldn't let him down. Every day he told himself the same thing: 'It's time I figured out who she really is. Was I wrong before, or am I wrong now? No, she's not stupid, she's a wonderful woman,' he sometimes told himself. 'She never makes a mistake, never says anything foolish. She says little, but what she says is always clear and simple—so she can't be stupid. She was never embarrassed and isn't embarrassed now, so she can't be a bad person!' He had often started thinking aloud or making reflections in her company, and she always responded either with a brief, appropriate remark—showing it didn't interest her—or with a silent look and smile that more clearly than anything demonstrated her superiority. She was right to consider all arguments meaningless compared to that smile.

She always greeted him with a radiantly trusting smile meant just for him, a smile with something more significant in it than the general smile that usually brightened her face. Pierre knew that everyone was waiting for him to say a certain word and cross a certain line, and he knew that sooner or later he would cross it. But an incomprehensible terror seized him at the thought of that dreadful step. A thousand times during that month and a half, feeling himself drawn closer and closer to the terrible precipice, Pierre said to himself: 'What am I doing? I need willpower. Don't I have any?'

He wanted to make a decision, but realized with dismay that in this particular matter he lacked the strength of will that he knew he possessed and had demonstrated before. Pierre was one of those people who are strong only when they feel completely innocent, and ever since that day at Anna Pavlovna's when he was overcome with desire while leaning over the snuffbox, an unacknowledged sense of guilt about that desire had paralyzed his will.

On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me...' and so on.
"So he never got past 'Sergei Kuzmich'?" asked one of the ladies.

"Exactly—not one word further," answered Prince Vasili, laughing. "'Sergei Kuzmich... From all sides... From all sides... Sergei Kuzmich...' Poor Vyazminitov couldn't get any further! He would start the letter over and over, but every time he said 'Sergei' he would sob, then 'Kuz-mich'—tears—and 'From all sides' would be swallowed up in sobs, and he couldn't go on. And then the handkerchief again, and again: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides...' and more tears, until finally someone else had to read it."
"Kuzmich... From all sides... and then tears," someone repeated, laughing.
"Don't be cruel," cried Anna Pavlovna from her end of the table, wagging her finger. "He is such a fine, worthy man, our dear Vyazminitov..."

Everyone laughed heartily. At the head of the table, where the honored guests sat, everyone seemed to be in high spirits, excited by many things at once. Only Pierre and Hélène sat quietly, almost at the far end, with a suppressed smile on both their faces—a smile that had nothing to do with Sergei Kuzmich, a smile of self-consciousness about their own feelings. But however much the others laughed, talked, joked, and enjoyed their Rhine wine, sauce, and ices, however much they avoided looking at the young couple and seemed oblivious to them, everyone could sense from the occasional glances cast their way that the story about Sergei Kuzmich, the laughter, and the food were all a performance—that the true focus of everyone's attention was Pierre and Hélène. Prince Vasili mimicked Sergei Kuzmich's sobbing while glancing at his daughter, and even as he laughed, his expression clearly said: 'Yes... it's moving along, it will all be settled today.' Anna Pavlovna scolded him on behalf of 'our dear Vyazminitov,' but in her eyes, which briefly met Pierre's, Prince Vasili could read congratulations for his future son-in-law and his daughter's happiness. The old princess sighed sadly as she offered wine to the lady beside her and glanced angrily at her daughter, her sigh seeming to say: 'Yes, there's nothing left for you and me but to sip wine, my dear, now that these young ones are being so bold and shamelessly happy.' 'What nonsense I'm thinking!' thought a diplomat, looking at the lovers' happy faces. 'That's happiness!'

Into this trivial, artificial society had entered the simple power of attraction between a healthy, handsome young man and woman. And this human feeling rose above everything else, towering over all their affected chatter. Jokes fell flat, news failed to interest, and the liveliness was clearly forced. Not just the guests but even the servants waiting at table seemed to sense this, forgetting their duties as they gazed at the beautiful Hélène with her radiant face and at Pierre's broad, red, happy—though uneasy—face. It was as if the very candlelight focused only on those two happy faces.

Pierre felt that he was at the center of it all, which both pleased and embarrassed him. He was like a man completely absorbed in something. He couldn't see, hear, or understand anything clearly. Only now and then, disconnected ideas and impressions from the real world would flash unexpectedly through his mind.

"So it's all settled!" he thought. "But how did it happen? So quickly! Now I know it's not just because of her or just because of me, but because of everyone—it has to happen. They're all expecting it, they're so certain it will happen that I can't, I simply can't, disappoint them. But how will it turn out? I don't know—but it will definitely happen!" thought Pierre, glancing at those dazzling shoulders so close to his eyes.

Or he would suddenly feel ashamed without knowing why. He felt awkward attracting everyone's attention and being considered a lucky man—him, with his plain face, being seen as some kind of Paris who had won a Helen. 'But it always is this way and has to be!' he reassured himself. 'And besides, what did I do to bring it about? How did it start? I came from Moscow with Prince Vasili. Then nothing happened. So why shouldn't I stay at his house? Then I played cards with her and picked up her handbag and went driving with her. How did it start? When did all this happen?' And here he was sitting beside her as her fiancé, seeing, hearing, and feeling her nearness, her breathing, her movements, her beauty. Then it would suddenly seem that it wasn't she who was so beautiful, but he himself, and that's why everyone was looking at him. Flattered by this general admiration, he would puff out his chest, lift his head, and rejoice in his good fortune. Then suddenly a familiar voice repeated something to him for the second time. But Pierre was so lost in thought that he didn't understand.
"I'm asking when you last heard from Bolkonsky," Prince Vasili repeated a third time. "How distracted you are, my dear fellow."

Prince Vasili smiled, and Pierre noticed that everyone was smiling at him and Hélène. 'Well, so what if everyone knows?' thought Pierre. 'So what? It's the truth!' And he gave his gentle, childlike smile, and Hélène smiled too.
"When did the letter arrive? Was it from Olmütz?" repeated Prince Vasili, pretending he needed to settle a debate.
"How can anyone talk or think about such trivial things?" thought Pierre.
"Yes, from Olmütz," he answered with a sigh.

After supper, Pierre and his partner followed the others into the drawing room. The guests began leaving, some without saying goodbye to Hélène. Others came up to her briefly, as if unwilling to distract her from something important, and hurried away, not letting her see them out. The diplomat left the drawing room in mournful silence, reflecting on the pointlessness of his diplomatic career compared to Pierre's happiness. The old general grumbled at his wife when she asked about his leg. 'What an old fool,' he thought. 'That Princess Hélène will still be beautiful at fifty.'
"I believe congratulations are in order," Anna Pavlovna whispered to the old princess, kissing her warmly. "If I didn't have this headache, I would have stayed longer."
The old princess didn't reply. She was tormented by jealousy of her daughter's happiness.

While the guests were leaving, Pierre remained alone with Hélène for a long time in the small drawing room where they had been sitting. He had often been alone with her during the past six weeks but had never spoken of love. Now he felt it was inevitable, yet he couldn't bring himself to take the final step. He felt ashamed; he felt he was occupying someone else's place beside Hélène. 'This happiness is not for you,' some inner voice whispered. 'This happiness is for those who don't have what you have inside you.'
But since he had to say something, he asked if she had enjoyed the party. She replied in her usual simple way that it had been one of the most pleasant name days she could remember.

Some close relatives hadn't left yet and were sitting in the large drawing room. Prince Vasili approached Pierre with slow steps. Pierre stood up and said it was getting late. Prince Vasili gave him a look of stern puzzlement, as if what Pierre had said was too strange to process. But then the severity melted away, and he pulled Pierre's hand down, made him sit, and smiled warmly.

"Well, Lelya?" he said, turning instantly to his daughter with the casual tenderness that parents naturally show children they've spoiled since birth—though Prince Vasili had only learned this manner by imitating other parents.
And he turned back to Pierre.
"Sergei Kuzmich—From all sides—" he said, unbuttoning the top button of his waistcoat.

Pierre smiled, but his smile showed he knew it wasn't the story about Sergei Kuzmich that Prince Vasili was really interested in, and Prince Vasili saw that Pierre knew this. He suddenly mumbled something and walked away. It seemed to Pierre that even the prince was flustered. The sight of this worldly old man's discomfort moved Pierre. He looked at Hélène, and she too seemed flustered, her expression seeming to say: 'Well, it's your own fault.'

"The step has to be taken, but I can't, I can't!" thought Pierre, and he started talking about unimportant things again, about Sergei Kuzmich, asking what the point of the story was, since he hadn't heard it properly. Hélène smiled and said she had missed it too.
When Prince Vasili returned to the drawing room, his wife, the princess, was whispering to the elderly lady about Pierre.
"Of course it's a brilliant match, but happiness, my dear..."
"Marriages are made in heaven," the elderly lady replied.
Prince Vasili walked past, pretending not to hear them, and sat down on a sofa in a far corner. He closed his eyes as if dozing. His head drooped forward, then he roused himself.
"Aline," he said to his wife, "go see what they're doing."
The princess went to the door, walked past it with a dignified, indifferent air, and peeked into the small drawing room. Pierre and Hélène were still sitting and talking, just as before.
"Still the same," she told her husband.

Prince Vasili frowned, his mouth twisting, his cheeks twitching, and his face taking on the coarse, unpleasant expression that was characteristic of him. He shook himself, stood up, threw back his head, and strode purposefully past the ladies into the small drawing room. He walked up to Pierre with quick, joyful steps. His face was so unusually triumphant that Pierre rose in alarm.

"Thank God!" said Prince Vasili. "My wife has told me everything!" He put one arm around Pierre and the other around his daughter. "My dear boy... Lelya... I am so pleased." His voice trembled. "I loved your father... and she will make you a good wife... God bless you!"
He embraced his daughter, then Pierre again, and kissed him. Tears actually wet his cheeks.
"Princess, come here!" he called out.

The old princess came in and wept too. The elderly lady dabbed at her eyes with a handkerchief. Pierre was kissed, and he kissed the beautiful Hélène's hand several times. After a while they were left alone again.

"All this had to happen and couldn't have been otherwise," thought Pierre, "so there's no point asking whether it's good or bad. It's good because it's definite, and I'm free of the old tormenting doubt." Pierre held his fiancée's hand in silence, watching her beautiful chest rise and fall.
"Hélène!" he said aloud, and paused.
"You're supposed to say something special at a moment like this," he thought, but couldn't remember what people say. He looked at her face. She moved closer. Her face flushed.
"Oh, take those off... those..." she said, pointing at his glasses.

Pierre took them off, and his eyes—besides the strange look that eyes always have right after glasses are removed—also had a frightened, questioning expression. He was about to lean over and kiss her hand, but with a quick, almost rough movement, she intercepted his lips with her own. Her face, with its altered, unpleasantly excited expression, startled Pierre.
"It's too late now, it's done. Besides, I love her," thought Pierre.
"I love you!" he said, remembering what you're supposed to say at such moments. But his words sounded so feeble that he felt embarrassed.
Six weeks later he was married and settled in Count Bezukhov's large, newly furnished Petersburg house—the happy owner, as everyone said, of a beautiful, celebrated wife and millions of rubles.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter III
paragraphs: Old Prince Bolkonsky received a letter from Prince Vasili in November 1805, announcing that he and his son would be visiting. 'I'm going on an inspection tour, and of course I won't mind an extra seventy miles to see you, my esteemed benefactor,' wrote Prince Vasili. 'My son Anatole is traveling with me on his way to the army, so I hope you'll allow him to personally express the deep respect that, following his father's example, he feels for you.'
"It seems we won't need to introduce Mary to society—suitors are coming to us on their own," the little princess carelessly remarked upon hearing the news.
Prince Bolkonsky frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks after the letter, Prince Vasili's servants arrived one evening ahead of him, and he and his son came the next day.

Old Bolkonsky had always had a low opinion of Prince Vasili's character, and even more so recently, since under Paul and Alexander, Prince Vasili had risen to high positions and honors. Now, from the hints in his letter and from the little princess's comments, he saw where this was heading, and his low opinion turned to contemptuous hostility. He snorted whenever Prince Vasili's name came up. On the day of the visit, the old prince was especially irritable and out of sorts. Whether he was in a bad mood because Prince Vasili was coming, or whether his bad mood made the visit especially annoying, he was difficult. That morning, Tikhon had already warned the architect not to go to the prince with his report.
"Hear how he's walking?" said Tikhon, drawing the architect's attention to the sound of the prince's footsteps. "Flat on his heels—we know what that means..."

Still, at nine o'clock, the prince put on his velvet coat with a sable collar and cap and went out for his usual walk. It had snowed the day before, and the path to the greenhouse that the prince always took had been swept clean. The marks of the broom were still visible in the snow, and a shovel had been left stuck in one of the snowbanks lining both sides of the path. The prince walked through the conservatories, the servants' quarters, and the outbuildings, frowning and silent.
"Can a sleigh get through?" he asked his steward, a dignified man who resembled his master in manner and appearance, as they walked back toward the house.
"The snow is deep. I'm having the drive swept, your honor."
The prince nodded and went up to the porch. 'Thank God,' thought the steward, 'the storm has passed!'
"It would have been hard to drive up, your honor," the steward added. "I heard that a minister is coming to visit, your honor."
The prince spun around and fixed his eyes on the steward, frowning.

"What? A minister? What minister? Who gave those orders?" he snapped in his shrill, harsh voice. "The road isn't swept for my daughter the princess, but for a minister! For me, there are no ministers!"
"Your honor, I thought—"

"You thought!" the prince shouted, his words coming faster and more garbled. "You thought!... Scoundrels! Idiots!... I'll teach you to think!" And he raised his walking stick and would have struck Alpatych, the steward, if the man hadn't instinctively jumped back. "Thought... Idiots..." the prince shouted.

But although Alpatych, frightened by his own boldness in dodging the blow, stepped forward with his bald head bowed submissively—or perhaps for that very reason—the prince, though he kept shouting "Idiots! Throw the snow back on the road!" didn't raise his stick again and hurried into the house.

Before dinner, Princess Mary and Mademoiselle Bourienne, who knew the prince was in a bad mood, stood waiting for him. Mademoiselle Bourienne had a bright expression that said, 'I know nothing, I'm the same as always,' while Princess Mary was pale, frightened, with downcast eyes. What she found hardest to bear was knowing that at times like these she should act like Mademoiselle Bourienne, but couldn't. She thought: 'If I act as if nothing's wrong, he'll think I don't care. But if I look sad and gloomy, he'll say—as he has before—that I'm sulking.'
The prince looked at his daughter's frightened face and snorted.
"Fool... or dunce!" he muttered.
"And the other one isn't here either. They've been gossiping," he thought, referring to the little princess, who wasn't in the dining room.
"Where is the princess?" he asked. "Hiding?"
"She isn't feeling well," Mademoiselle Bourienne answered with a bright smile. "She won't be coming down. It's natural in her condition."
"Hm! Hm!" the prince muttered, sitting down.

His plate seemed not quite clean to him. Pointing at a spot, he flung it away. Tikhon caught it and passed it to a footman. The little princess wasn't actually ill, but she was so terrified of the prince that, hearing he was in a bad temper, she had decided not to come down.
"I'm worried about the baby," she told Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Who knows what a fright could do."

In general, life at Bald Hills meant constant fear for the little princess, mixed with a feeling of dislike for the old prince that she didn't acknowledge because the fear was so much stronger. The prince returned that dislike, but it was overwhelmed by his contempt for her. Once the little princess had settled in at Bald Hills, she took a particular liking to Mademoiselle Bourienne, spent whole days with her, asked her to sleep in her room, and often talked with her about the old prince, criticizing him.

"So we're going to have visitors, Prince?" said Mademoiselle Bourienne, unfolding her white napkin with her pink fingers. "His Excellency Prince Vasili Kuragin and his son, I understand?" she said, as if asking for confirmation.

"Hm—his excellency is a lightweight... I got him his position," the prince said dismissively. "Why his son is coming, I have no idea. Maybe Princess Elizabeth and Princess Mary know. I don't want him." He looked at his blushing daughter. "Are you unwell today? Eh? Scared of the 'minister,' as that fool Alpatych called him this morning?"
"No, Father."

Although Mademoiselle Bourienne had chosen her topic poorly, she didn't stop talking. She chattered about the conservatories and a flower that had just bloomed. After the soup, the prince became more pleasant.
After dinner he went to visit his daughter-in-law. The little princess was sitting at a small table chatting with Masha, her maid. She turned pale when she saw her father-in-law.
She had changed a great deal. She was now plain rather than pretty. Her cheeks had hollowed, her lip curled up, and her eyes were drawn down.
"Yes, I feel some pressure," she said in answer to the prince's question about how she was feeling.
"Do you need anything?"
"No, thank you, Father."
"Very well then."
He left the room and went to the vestibule, where Alpatych stood with his head bowed.
"Was the snow put back?"
"Yes, your excellency. Forgive me, for heaven's sake... It was just my stupidity."
"Fine, fine," the prince interrupted, and with his strange, forced laugh, he held out his hand for Alpatych to kiss, then went to his study.

Prince Vasili arrived that evening. He was met on the drive by coachmen and servants who, shouting loudly, dragged his sleighs up to one of the lodges over the road that had been deliberately piled with snow.
Prince Vasili and Anatole were given separate rooms.

Anatole, having taken off his coat, sat with arms crossed before a table, smilingly and absent-mindedly fixing his large, handsome eyes on one corner. He viewed his entire life as one continuous round of entertainment that someone, for some reason, had to provide for him. He regarded this visit to a grumpy old man and a rich, ugly heiress the same way. It might all turn out quite nicely and amusingly. 'And why not marry her if she really has that much money? That never hurts,' thought Anatole.

He shaved and perfumed himself with the care and elegance that had become second nature, and with his handsome head held high, entered his father's room with his naturally cheerful and confident air. Prince Vasili's two valets were busy dressing him. He looked around with great animation and gave his son a friendly nod as he entered, as if to say: 'Yes, that's exactly how I want you to look.'
"Seriously though, Father, is she really that ugly?" Anatole asked, as if picking up a conversation they'd had many times on the journey.
"Enough! Don't be ridiculous! Above all, try to be respectful and careful with the old prince."
"If he starts making trouble, I'm leaving," said Anatole. "I can't stand those old men! Right?"
"Remember, everything depends on this for you."

Meanwhile, it wasn't just the servants who knew the minister and his son had arrived—both their appearances had been described in minute detail. Princess Mary sat alone in her room, trying in vain to calm her anxiety.

"Why did they write? Why did Lise tell me about it? It can never happen!" she said, looking at herself in the mirror. "How will I walk into the drawing room? Even if I like him, I can't be myself with him now." The mere thought of her father's look filled her with dread. The little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne had already received from Masha, the lady's maid, a thorough report on how handsome the minister's son was, with his rosy cheeks and dark eyebrows, and how his father had barely managed to drag his legs upstairs while the son had bounded up like an eagle, three steps at a time. With this intelligence in hand, the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne, whose chattering voices had been audible from the hallway, went into Princess Mary's room.
"Did you know they've arrived, Marie?" said the little princess, waddling in and sinking heavily into an armchair.

She had changed out of her usual loose morning gown and put on one of her best dresses. Her hair was done up and her face was lively—though this couldn't hide how much thinner and paler she had become. Dressed as she used to be in Petersburg society, it was even more obvious how much plainer she looked now. Some subtle touch had been added to Mademoiselle Bourienne's outfit that made her fresh, pretty face even more appealing.

"What—are you going to stay like that, dear princess?" she began. "They're going to announce the gentlemen in the drawing room any minute and we'll have to go down, and you haven't done anything with yourself!"

The little princess jumped up, rang for the maid, and with cheerful energy began planning how to dress Princess Mary. Princess Mary's pride was wounded by the fact that a suitor's arrival excited her, and even more by her companions' complete inability to imagine she might feel differently about it. To tell them she was embarrassed—for herself and for them—would be to reveal her agitation. To refuse their help would only prolong their teasing and insistence. She blushed, her beautiful eyes dimmed, red blotches appeared on her face, and it took on the unattractive, long-suffering expression it so often wore as she submitted to Mademoiselle Bourienne and Lise. Both women sincerely tried to make her pretty. She was so plain that neither could see her as a rival, so they set about dressing her with genuine conviction—the unshakable female belief that clothes can make any face pretty.

"No, really, dear, this dress won't do," said Lise, studying Princess Mary from a distance. "You have a maroon dress—go get it. Seriously! Your whole life might depend on this. But this one is too light, it's not right for you!"

It wasn't the dress but Princess Mary's face and whole figure that weren't attractive. But neither Mademoiselle Bourienne nor the little princess could see this. They still believed that if a blue ribbon were placed in her hair, the hair pinned up, and the blue scarf lowered on the best maroon dress, everything would be fine. They forgot that the anxious face and the figure couldn't be changed, and that no matter how much they altered the setting and accessories around that face, it would still look sad and plain. After two or three outfit changes—to which Princess Mary meekly submitted—once her hair had been piled on top of her head (a style that completely altered and worsened her appearance) and she had put on a maroon dress with a pale-blue scarf, the little princess circled her twice, adjusting a fold here, straightening the scarf there, tilting her head this way and that.

"No, it won't work," she said firmly, clasping her hands. "No, Marie, this dress really doesn't suit you. I prefer you in your little gray everyday dress. Please, do it for my sake. Katie," she called to the maid, "bring the princess her gray dress, and you'll see, Mademoiselle Bourienne, how I'll fix it up." She smiled with the anticipated pleasure of an artist.

But when Katie brought the gray dress, Princess Mary sat motionless before the mirror, staring at her face. In the reflection she could see her eyes filling with tears and her mouth quivering, about to burst into sobs.
"Come, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "just one more little effort."
The little princess took the dress from the maid and came over to Princess Mary.
"Now we'll make something simple and flattering," she said.
The three voices—hers, Mademoiselle Bourienne's, and Katie's, who was laughing at something—blended together in a cheerful sound, like birdsong.
"No, leave me alone," said Princess Mary.

Her voice sounded so serious and so sad that the birdsong stopped at once. They looked at her beautiful, large, thoughtful eyes, shining with tears and unspoken thoughts, gazing imploringly at them—and understood that insisting would be useless, even cruel.

"At least change your hairstyle," said the little princess. "Didn't I tell you," she added, turning reproachfully to Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that Mary's face doesn't suit that style at all? Not at all! Please change it."
"Leave me alone, please leave me alone! It's all the same to me," answered a voice struggling with tears.

Mademoiselle Bourienne and the little princess had to admit to themselves that Princess Mary looked very plain like this—worse than usual—but it was too late. She gazed at them with an expression they both knew well: thoughtful and sad. This look never frightened anyone (she was never intimidating), but they knew that when it appeared, she became silent and nothing could change her mind.
"You will change it, won't you?" said Lise. When Princess Mary didn't answer, she left the room.

Princess Mary was left alone. She didn't do as Lise asked; she not only kept her hair as it was but didn't even glance in the mirror. Letting her arms fall helplessly, she sat with downcast eyes and lost herself in thought. In her imagination, a husband appeared—a man, strong, commanding, and strangely attractive—and carried her away into a completely different, happy world. She imagined a child, her own—like the one she had seen yesterday in her nurse's daughter's arms—at her breast, with the husband standing beside her, gazing tenderly at her and the baby. 'But no, it's impossible—I'm too ugly,' she thought.
"Please come to tea. The prince will be out in a moment," came the maid's voice from the door.

She stirred and was appalled at what she had been thinking. Before going downstairs, she went into the room where the icons hung and stood before the dark face of a large icon of the Savior, lit by a lamp, her hands folded in prayer. A painful doubt filled her soul. Could the joy of love—earthly love for a man—really be meant for her? In her dreams of marriage, Princess Mary imagined happiness and children, but her deepest, most hidden longing was for earthly love. The harder she tried to conceal this feeling from others and from herself, the stronger it grew. 'Oh God,' she said, 'how can I overcome these temptations? How can I give up these sinful dreams and peacefully fulfill Your will?' And as soon as she asked the question, God answered in her own heart. 'Desire nothing for yourself. Seek nothing. Be not anxious or envious. The future—both mankind's and your own—must remain hidden from you. But live so that you are ready for anything. If God wills that you be tested in marriage, be ready to fulfill His will.' With this comforting thought—though still harboring hope for the fulfillment of her forbidden earthly longing—Princess Mary sighed, crossed herself, and went downstairs, thinking not of her dress or hairstyle or how she would enter or what she would say. What did any of that matter compared to the will of God, without whose care not a single hair falls from anyone's head?

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: When Princess Mary came downstairs, Prince Vasili and his son were already in the drawing room, talking with the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne. As she entered with her heavy step, walking on her heels, the gentlemen and Mademoiselle Bourienne stood up, and the little princess pointed her out to the guests: 'Here's Marie!' Princess Mary saw them all and registered every detail. She saw Prince Vasili's face go serious for an instant when he noticed her, then immediately break into a smile again. She saw the little princess watching curiously for the impression 'Marie' would make. She saw Mademoiselle Bourienne with her ribbon and pretty face, looking unusually animated, her eyes fixed on him. But him she couldn't really see—she only saw something large, brilliant, and handsome moving toward her. Prince Vasili approached first, and she kissed the bold forehead that bent over her hand, answering his question by saying that she remembered him perfectly well. Then Anatole came up. She still couldn't see him clearly. She only felt a soft hand take hers firmly, and her lips touched a white forehead framed by beautiful light-brown hair that smelled of pomade. When she finally looked up, she was struck by his beauty. Anatole stood with his right thumb hooked under a button of his uniform, his chest out, his back straight, gently shifting his weight on one foot, his head tilted slightly, looking at the princess with a beaming face—not speaking and obviously not thinking about her at all. Anatole wasn't quick-witted or eloquent in conversation, but he had the invaluable social gift of composure and unshakable self-assurance. If a man who lacks confidence stays silent at a first meeting, betraying awareness of the awkwardness and anxiety to fill it, the effect is bad. But Anatole was silent, he shifted his weight, and he smiled while studying the princess's hair arrangement. He clearly could have stayed silent like this for a very long time. 'If anyone finds this silence uncomfortable, they can talk, but I don't feel like it,' he seemed to say. Beyond this, in his manner with women, Anatole had a way that particularly inspired curiosity, awe, and even love—a casual awareness of his own superiority. It was as though he were saying to them: 'I know you. I know you very well. But why should I bother with you? You'd be delighted, of course.' Perhaps he didn't actually think this when meeting women—most likely he didn't, since he rarely thought much at all—but his looks and behavior gave that impression. The princess sensed it, and as if wanting to show that she didn't even expect to interest him, she turned to his father. The conversation was lively and animated, thanks to Princess Lise's voice and her little downy lip curving over her white teeth. She greeted Prince Vasili with the playful manner common to chatty, lively people—the kind that assumes a shared history of private jokes and fond memories between speaker and listener, even when no such history exists. Prince Vasili played along easily, and the little princess also drew Anatole, whom she barely knew, into these entertaining recollections of things that had never happened. Mademoiselle Bourienne joined in too, and even Princess Mary felt herself pleasantly pulled into these cheerful, fictional reminiscences.

"Here at least we'll have you all to ourselves, dear prince," the little princess said to Prince Vasili in French. "It's not like at Annette's parties, where you always ran off. You remember dear Annette!"
Anna Pavlovna.
"Oh, but you won't lecture me about politics like Annette!"
"And our little tea table?"
"Oh, yes!"

"Why were you never at Annette's?" the little princess asked Anatole. "Oh, I know, I know," she said with a sly look, "your brother Hippolyte told me all about your adventures. Oh!" And she wagged her finger at him. "I've even heard about your escapades in Paris!"

"And didn't Hippolyte tell you," asked Prince Vasili, turning to his son and grabbing the little princess's arm as if she were about to escape, "how he pined for the dear princess, and how she showed him the door? Oh, she's a pearl among women, princess," he added, turning to Princess Mary.
When Paris was mentioned, Mademoiselle Bourienne seized the chance to join in.

She asked if it had been long since Anatole left Paris and whether he had enjoyed it there. Anatole answered the Frenchwoman readily and, studying her with a smile, chatted with her about her homeland. When he noticed the pretty little Bourienne, Anatole decided that life at Bald Hills might not be boring after all. 'Not bad at all!' he thought, looking her over. 'Not bad at all, that little companion! Hopefully she'll come along when we're married. She's quite charming.'
The little one is charming.

The old prince took his time dressing in his study, frowning and thinking about what to do. These visitors annoyed him. 'What are Prince Vasili and that son of his to me? Prince Vasili is a shallow braggart, and his son is probably a fine specimen,' he grumbled to himself. What really angered him was that the visit forced him to face a question he always tried to suppress, one about which he was always dishonest with himself: could he ever bring himself to give up his daughter and let her marry? The prince never asked himself the question directly, knowing he would have to answer it honestly, and honesty clashed not just with his feelings but with the very possibility of his life. Life without Princess Mary—little as he seemed to value her—was unthinkable to him. 'Why should she marry?' he thought. 'To be miserable, that's certain. Look at Lise, married to Andrew—you'd think a better husband couldn't be found these days—but is she happy? And who would marry Mary for love? She's plain and awkward! They'd only want her for her connections and money. There are plenty of women living unmarried, and they're happier for it.' So thought Prince Bolkonsky while dressing. Yet the question he kept putting off demanded an immediate answer. Prince Vasili had brought his son with the obvious intention of proposing, and today or tomorrow he would likely expect an answer. His birth and social position were acceptable. 'Well, I have nothing against it,' the prince said to himself, 'but he has to be worthy of her. And that's what we'll find out.'
"That's what we'll see! That's what we'll see!" he said aloud.

He entered the drawing room with his usual brisk step, glancing quickly around the room. He noticed the little princess's change of dress, Mademoiselle Bourienne's ribbon, Princess Mary's unflattering hairstyle, Mademoiselle Bourienne's and Anatole's smiles, and his daughter's loneliness amid the general conversation. 'Dressed herself up like a fool!' he thought irritably, looking at her. 'No shame! And he ignores her!'
He went straight up to Prince Vasili.
"Well! Hello! Hello! Good to see you!"
"Friendship laughs at distance," Prince Vasili began in his usual rapid, confident, familiar tone. "Here is my second son. Please be kind to him."
Prince Bolkonsky studied Anatole.
"Fine young man! Fine young man!" he said. "Well, come give me a kiss." And he offered his cheek.
Anatole kissed the old man and studied him with curiosity and perfect composure, waiting for the eccentric behavior his father had warned him about.

Prince Bolkonsky sat down in his usual corner of the sofa and, pulling up an armchair for Prince Vasili, gestured for him to sit. He began asking about politics and the news, seeming to listen carefully to what Prince Vasili said while constantly glancing at Princess Mary.
"So they're writing from Potsdam already?" he said, repeating Prince Vasili's last words. Then he suddenly got up and walked over to his daughter.

"Is that how you dress for visitors, eh?" he said. "Very nice, very nice! You've done your hair in a new way for the guests, and in front of the guests I'm telling you: never again dare change your appearance without my permission."
"It was my fault, Father," the little princess interjected, blushing.
"You may do as you please," Prince Bolkonsky told his daughter-in-law with a bow, "but she doesn't need to make herself look ridiculous—she's plain enough as it is."
And he sat down again, paying no more attention to his daughter, who was in tears.
"On the contrary, that hairstyle suits the princess very well," said Prince Vasili.
"Now then, young prince—what's your name?" said Prince Bolkonsky, turning to Anatole. "Come here, let's talk and get to know each other."
"Now the fun begins," thought Anatole, sitting down beside the old prince with a smile.

"Well, my boy, I hear you were educated abroad—not taught to read by the village deacon, like your father and me. Tell me, are you serving in the Horse Guards?" asked the old man, scrutinizing Anatole closely.
"No, I've been transferred to a line regiment," said Anatole, barely suppressing a laugh.
"Ah! Good thing. So, my boy, you want to serve the Tsar and the country? It's wartime. A fine fellow like you should serve. Well, are you heading to the front?"
"No, Prince, our regiment has moved to the front, but I'm attached... what am I attached to, Papa?" said Anatole, turning to his father with a laugh.
"Splendid soldier, splendid! 'What am I attached to!' Ha, ha, ha!" laughed Prince Bolkonsky, and Anatole laughed even harder. Suddenly the old prince frowned.
"You may go," he told Anatole.
Anatole returned to the ladies with a smile.
"So you had him educated abroad, Prince Vasili?" said the old prince.
"I did my best for him, and I can assure you the education there is much better than ours."

"Yes, everything is different nowadays, everything has changed. The boy's a fine fellow, a fine fellow! Well, come with me." He took Prince Vasili by the arm and led him to his study. As soon as they were alone, Prince Vasili laid out his hopes and intentions.

"What, do you think I'd stop her? That I can't bear to part with her?" the old prince said angrily. "What an idea! I'm ready tomorrow! Only let me tell you, I want to know my future son-in-law better. You know my principles—everything in the open! I'll ask her tomorrow, with you there. If she's willing, then he can stay. He can stay and I'll observe him." He snorted. "Let her marry—it's all the same to me!" he shouted in the same piercing voice he had used when saying goodbye to his son.

"I'll be frank with you," said Prince Vasili, in the tone of a cunning man who has decided there's no point being cunning with someone so sharp. "You know people, you see right through them. Anatole is no genius, but he's an honest, good-hearted young man—an excellent son and kinsman."
"Fine, fine, we'll see!"

As always happens when women live alone for a long time without male company, the arrival of Anatole made all three women of Prince Bolkonsky's household feel that their lives up to that point hadn't been real. Their powers of thinking, feeling, and observing increased tenfold, and their existence, which seemed to have been spent in darkness, was suddenly filled with new, meaningful light.

Princess Mary became completely oblivious to her face and hair. The open, handsome face of the man who might become her husband consumed all her attention. He seemed to her kind, brave, determined, manly, and generous. She felt certain of it. Thousands of dreams about family life rose endlessly in her imagination. She tried to push them away and hide them.

"But am I being too cold with him?" the princess wondered. "I'm trying to hold back because deep down I already feel too close to him. But he can't know what I'm thinking and might believe I don't like him."
And Princess Mary tried—but couldn't manage—to be warm to her new guest. 'Poor girl, she's hopelessly ugly!' thought Anatole.

Mademoiselle Bourienne, also stirred by Anatole's arrival, had quite different thoughts. A beautiful young woman with no real status, no family, not even a country of her own, she certainly hadn't intended to devote her life to serving Prince Bolkonsky, reading aloud to him, and being Princess Mary's companion. Mademoiselle Bourienne had long been waiting for a Russian prince who would recognize at a glance her superiority over the plain, badly dressed, ungainly Russian princesses, fall in love with her, and carry her away. And here at last was a Russian prince. She had a story, heard from her aunt but embellished in her own imagination, that she loved to replay in her mind. It was about a girl who had been seduced, and whose poor mother appeared to reproach her for giving herself to a man without marriage. Mademoiselle Bourienne was often moved to tears as she imagined telling this story to him, her seducer. And now he, a real Russian prince, had appeared. He would carry her off, and then her poor mother would appear, and he would marry her. So her future took shape in Mademoiselle Bourienne's mind even as she chatted with Anatole about Paris. It wasn't calculation guiding her—she didn't even stop to think about what she should do—but all of this had been familiar to her for so long that now, with Anatole present, it simply arranged itself around him, and she wished and tried to please him as much as possible.

The little princess, like a retired warhorse hearing the trumpet, unconsciously and completely forgetting her condition, prepared for the familiar thrill of flirtation—without ulterior motive or inner struggle, with simple, lighthearted pleasure.

Although Anatole usually played the role of a man weary of being chased by women, his vanity was flattered by the sight of his power over these three women. Besides that, he was beginning to feel for the pretty, provocative Mademoiselle Bourienne that passionate, animal desire that tended to seize him suddenly and drive him to the most reckless behavior.

After tea, the group moved to the sitting room and Princess Mary was asked to play the clavichord. Anatole, laughing and in high spirits, leaned on his elbows facing her, next to Mademoiselle Bourienne. Princess Mary felt his gaze with a painful, joyful emotion. Her favorite sonata carried her into a deeply poetic inner world, and the look she felt on her made that world even more beautiful. But Anatole's eyes, though aimed at her, were actually focused on Mademoiselle Bourienne's little foot, which he was nudging with his own under the clavichord. Mademoiselle Bourienne was looking at Princess Mary too, and in her lovely eyes there was an expression of fearful excitement and hope that was new to the princess.

"How she loves me!" thought Princess Mary. "How happy I am now, and how happy I could be with such a friend and such a husband! A husband? Is it really possible?" she thought, not daring to look at his face but still feeling his eyes on her.

That evening, after supper, as everyone was about to retire, Anatole kissed Princess Mary's hand. She didn't know where she found the courage, but she looked straight into his handsome face as it came close to her nearsighted eyes. After Princess Mary, he went up and kissed Mademoiselle Bourienne's hand. (This wasn't proper etiquette, but he did everything with such easy confidence!) Mademoiselle Bourienne blushed and gave the princess a frightened glance.

"What sensitivity!" thought the princess. "Is it possible that Amélie"—Mademoiselle Bourienne—"thinks I could be jealous of her and fail to appreciate her pure devotion to me?" She went over and warmly kissed her. Anatole then went to kiss the little princess's hand.
"No! No! No! When your father writes to tell me you've been behaving yourself, I'll let you kiss my hand. Not before!" she said. And with a teasing smile, wagging her finger, she left the room.
